claim: The bacteriophage population is large, dynamic, ancient, and genetically diverse.
source: The bacteriophage population is large, dynamic, ancient, and genetically diverse.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general characterization of bacteriophages, drawing from established scientific knowledge.

claim: Limited genomic information shows that phage genomes are mosaic.
source: Limited genomic information shows that phage genomes are mosaic, and the genetic architecture of phage populations remains ill-defined.
evidence: This statement references existing genomic information about phage genome structure.

claim: 627 phages of Mycobacterium smegmatis were isolated, sequenced, and compared.
source: To understand the population structure of phages infecting a single host strain, we isolated, sequenced, and compared 627 phages of Mycobacterium smegmatis.
evidence: This describes the experimental work performed in this study.

claim: The genetic diversity of the 627 mycobacteriophages is considerable.
source: Their genetic diversity is considerable, and there are 28 distinct genomic types (clusters) with related nucleotide sequences.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of the sequenced phages.

claim: There are 28 distinct genomic types (clusters) with related nucleotide sequences among the 627 mycobacteriophages.
source: Their genetic diversity is considerable, and there are 28 distinct genomic types (clusters) with related nucleotide sequences.
evidence: This is a direct result from the clustering analysis of the phage genomes.

claim: Amino acid sequence comparisons show pervasive genomic mosaicism in mycobacteriophages.
source: However, amino acid sequence comparisons show pervasive genomic mosaicism, and quantification of inter-cluster and intra-cluster relatedness reveals a continuum of genetic diversity, albeit with uneven representation of different phages.
evidence: This is based on amino acid sequence comparison data from the study.

claim: Quantification of inter-cluster and intra-cluster relatedness reveals a continuum of genetic diversity with uneven representation of different phages.
source: However, amino acid sequence comparisons show pervasive genomic mosaicism, and quantification of inter-cluster and intra-cluster relatedness reveals a continuum of genetic diversity, albeit with uneven representation of different phages.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the quantitative analysis of cluster relationships.

claim: Rarefaction analysis shows that the mycobacteriophage population is not closed.
source: Furthermore, rarefaction analysis shows that the mycobacteriophage population is not closed, and there is a constant influx of genes from other sources.
evidence: This is based on rarefaction analysis performed in the study.

claim: There is a constant influx of genes from other sources into the mycobacteriophage population.
source: Furthermore, rarefaction analysis shows that the mycobacteriophage population is not closed, and there is a constant influx of genes from other sources.
evidence: This is inferred from the rarefaction analysis results.

claim: Phage isolation and analysis was performed by a large consortium of academic institutions.
source: Phage isolation and analysis was performed by a large consortium of academic institutions, illustrating the substantial benefits of a disseminated, structured program involving large numbers of freshman undergraduates in scientific discovery.
evidence: This describes the organizational structure of the research program.

claim: Phages are the most abundant organisms in the biosphere.
source: Phages are the most abundant organisms in the biosphere, and the ∼1031 tailed phage particles participate in ∼1023 infections per second on a global scale, with the entire population turning over every few days (Suttle, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Suttle, 2007.

claim: Approximately 10^31 tailed phage particles participate in approximately 10^23 infections per second on a global scale.
source: Phages are the most abundant organisms in the biosphere, and the ∼1031 tailed phage particles participate in ∼1023 infections per second on a global scale, with the entire population turning over every few days (Suttle, 2007).
evidence: This quantitative estimate is supported by citation to Suttle, 2007.

claim: The entire bacteriophage population turns over every few days.
source: Phages are the most abundant organisms in the biosphere, and the ∼1031 tailed phage particles participate in ∼1023 infections per second on a global scale, with the entire population turning over every few days (Suttle, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Suttle, 2007.

claim: Comparisons of virion structures suggest that the bacteriophage population is extremely old.
source: The population is not only vast and dynamic, but comparisons of virion structures suggest that it is also extremely old (Krupovic and Bamford, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Krupovic and Bamford, 2010.

claim: There are approximately 2000 completely sequenced bacteriophage genomes in the GenBank database.
source: To date, there are approximately 2000 completely sequenced bacteriophage genomes in the GenBank database, a small number relative to the more than 30,000 sequenced prokaryotic genomes (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genome/browse/), in spite of phage genomes being only 1–5% of the size of their host genomes.
evidence: This is a factual statement about database contents at the time of writing.

claim: There are more than 30,000 sequenced prokaryotic genomes.
source: To date, there are approximately 2000 completely sequenced bacteriophage genomes in the GenBank database, a small number relative to the more than 30,000 sequenced prokaryotic genomes (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genome/browse/), in spite of phage genomes being only 1–5% of the size of their host genomes.
evidence: This is a factual statement about database contents at the time of writing.

claim: Phage genomes are only 1-5% of the size of their host genomes.
source: To date, there are approximately 2000 completely sequenced bacteriophage genomes in the GenBank database, a small number relative to the more than 30,000 sequenced prokaryotic genomes (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genome/browse/), in spite of phage genomes being only 1–5% of the size of their host genomes.
evidence: This is a general statement about relative genome sizes based on established knowledge.

claim: Double-stranded DNA tailed phages are proposed to have evolved with common ancestry but with different phages having differential access to a large common gene pool.
source: Double-stranded DNA tailed phages are proposed to have evolved with common ancestry but with different phages having differential access to a large common gene pool (Hendrix et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hendrix et al., 1999.

claim: Phage genomes are typified by their mosaic architectures generated by gene loss and gain through horizontal genetic exchange.
source: Phage genomes are typified by their mosaic architectures generated by gene loss and gain through horizontal genetic exchange; however, the parameters influencing access to the common gene pool are numerous and likely include host range, genome size, replication mode, and life style (temperate vs lytic).
evidence: This is a general statement about phage genome architecture based on established knowledge.

claim: Parameters influencing access to the common gene pool likely include host range, genome size, replication mode, and life style (temperate vs lytic).
source: Phage genomes are typified by their mosaic architectures generated by gene loss and gain through horizontal genetic exchange; however, the parameters influencing access to the common gene pool are numerous and likely include host range, genome size, replication mode, and life style (temperate vs lytic).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about factors affecting gene pool access.

claim: Migration to new hosts is probably common in bacteriophages.
source: Migration to new hosts is probably common, but is affected by local host diversity and mutation rates, as well as resistance mechanisms such as receptor availability, restriction, CRISPRs, and abortive infection systems (Buckling and Brockhurst, 2012; Jacobs-Sera et al., 2012; Hoskisson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Host migration in phages is affected by local host diversity and mutation rates, as well as resistance mechanisms such as receptor availability, restriction, CRISPRs, and abortive infection systems.
source: Migration to new hosts is probably common, but is affected by local host diversity and mutation rates, as well as resistance mechanisms such as receptor availability, restriction, CRISPRs, and abortive infection systems (Buckling and Brockhurst, 2012; Jacobs-Sera et al., 2012; Hoskisson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Buckling and Brockhurst, 2012; Jacobs-Sera et al., 2012; Hoskisson et al., 2015.

claim: Constraints on gene acquisition may be imposed by synteny, particularly among virion structural genes.
source: Constraints on gene acquisition may also be imposed by synteny—particularly among virion structural genes—and by size limits of DNA packaging (Juhala et al., 2000; Hatfull and Hendrix, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Juhala et al., 2000; Hatfull and Hendrix, 2011.

claim: Constraints on gene acquisition may be imposed by size limits of DNA packaging.
source: Constraints on gene acquisition may also be imposed by synteny—particularly among virion structural genes—and by size limits of DNA packaging (Juhala et al., 2000; Hatfull and Hendrix, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Juhala et al., 2000; Hatfull and Hendrix, 2011.

claim: Mycobacteriophages can be sorted by nucleotide sequence and gene content comparisons into groups of closely related genomes referred to as 'clusters'.
source: We have previously described comparative analyses of modest numbers of mycobacteriophages and shown that they can be sorted by nucleotide sequence and gene content comparisons into groups of closely related genomes referred to as 'clusters' (designated Cluster A, B, C, etc.); phages without any close relatives are referred to as 'singletons'.
evidence: This describes a previously established classification method.

claim: Phages without any close relatives are referred to as 'singletons'.
source: We have previously described comparative analyses of modest numbers of mycobacteriophages and shown that they can be sorted by nucleotide sequence and gene content comparisons into groups of closely related genomes referred to as 'clusters' (designated Cluster A, B, C, etc.); phages without any close relatives are referred to as 'singletons'.
evidence: This defines terminology used in phage classification.

claim: Some mycobacteriophage clusters can be further divided into subclusters according to nucleotide sequence relatedness.
source: Some of the clusters can be further divided into subclusters (e.g., Subcluster A1, A2, A3, etc.) according to nucleotide sequence relatedness (Pedulla et al., 2003; Hatfull et al., 2006, 2010; Pope et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Mycobacteriophage genomes are mosaic whereby individual phages are constructed as assemblages of modules, many of which are single genes.
source: The genomes are mosaic whereby individual phages are constructed as assemblages of modules, many of which are single genes (Pedulla et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pedulla et al., 2003.

claim: Each mycobacteriophage cluster has features particular to that cluster.
source: Each mycobacteriophage cluster has features particular to that cluster (e.g., regulatory systems, repeated sequences, tRNA genes, etc. [Pope et al., 2011a, 2011b, 2013, 2014a, 2014b]), but because of the pervasive mosaicism, the relationships among phages within clusters and between clusters are complex.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies by Pope et al.

claim: Collections of phages have been isolated on other hosts such as Bacillus spp., Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas spp., Propionibacterium spp. and Staphylococcus spp.
source: Collections of phages have been isolated on other hosts such as Bacillus spp., Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas spp., Propionibacterium spp. and Staphylococcus spp. (Kwan et al., 2005, 2006; Kropinski et al., 2007; Marinelli et al., 2012; Hatfull et al., 2013; Grose and Casjens, 2014; Grose et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2014) and these can be similarly divided into clusters based on DNA similarity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Analysis of 337 phages infecting 31 bacterial species within the Enterobacteriaceae reveals 56 clusters of phage genomes.
source: Recent analysis of 337 phages infecting 31 bacterial species within the Enterobacteriaceae (Grose and Casjens, 2014) reveals 56 clusters of phage genomes.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Grose and Casjens, 2014.

claim: Viral metagenomic studies typically generate few complete genome sequences or any specific information relating viral genomes to specific bacterial hosts.
source: Viral metagenomic studies provide valuable insights into phage diversity and population dynamics, but typically generate few complete genome sequences or any specific information relating viral genomes to specific bacterial hosts (Hambly and Suttle, 2005; Rodriguez-Brito et al., 2010; Mokili et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple metagenomic studies.

claim: A recent analysis of Synechococcus phages using metagenomic analysis coupled with viral tagging showed that there are multiple 'populations' of these phages.
source: A recent analysis of Synechococcus phages using metagenomic analysis coupled with viral tagging showed that there are multiple 'populations' of these phages (similar to the clusters described above), but suggested that these represent distinct groups of related phages rather than a continuous spectrum of diversity (Deng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Deng et al., 2014.

claim: The Synechococcus phage analysis suggested that phage populations represent distinct groups of related phages rather than a continuous spectrum of diversity.
source: A recent analysis of Synechococcus phages using metagenomic analysis coupled with viral tagging showed that there are multiple 'populations' of these phages (similar to the clusters described above), but suggested that these represent distinct groups of related phages rather than a continuous spectrum of diversity (Deng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Deng et al., 2014.

claim: Prior predictions suggest that the phage population as a whole likely spans a continuum of diversity with uneven representation of different groups of related phages because of genomic mosaicism.
source: This differs from prior predictions that the phage population as a whole likely spans a continuum of diversity—albeit with uneven representation of different groups of related phages—because of genomic mosaicism (Hendrix, 2003; Hatfull, 2010, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hendrix, 2003; Hatfull, 2010, 2012.

claim: The comparative analysis of mycobacteriophage genomes demonstrates that they represent a spectrum of diversity and do not constitute discrete populations.
source: Here we describe the comparative analysis of a large number of completely sequenced mycobacteriophage genomes and demonstrate that they represent a spectrum of diversity and do not constitute discrete populations.
evidence: This is a main conclusion from the data analysis presented in the study.

claim: Rarefaction analyses of mycobacteriophage genes are consistent with populations of gene families shared among mycobacteriophages being augmented by the introduction of new gene families from outside sources.
source: Rarefaction analyses of their constituent genes are consistent with populations of gene families shared among mycobacteriophages being augmented by the introduction of new gene families from outside sources.
evidence: This is based on rarefaction analysis performed in the study.

claim: A course-based research experience (CRE) can be successfully implemented at large scale without compromising the authenticity or richness of a scientific investigation imbued with discovery and project ownership.
source: The assembling of a large and highly informative collection of bacteriophages by a consortium of students and faculty at multiple institutions demonstrates that a course-based research experience (CRE) can be successfully implemented at large scale without compromising the authenticity or richness of a scientific investigation imbued with discovery and project ownership.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the educational model based on the successful execution of the project.

claim: The 2012 report from the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology (PCAST) focused on the poor retention of undergraduate students in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) as an impediment to meeting US economic demands.
source: The 2012 report from the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology (PCAST) focused on the poor retention of undergraduate students in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) as an impediment to meeting US economic demands (PCAST, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to PCAST, 2012.

claim: One of the PCAST recommendations is to replace traditional introductory laboratory courses with research-based experiences that would inspire freshman students and promote STEM retention.
source: One of the PCAST recommendations is to replace traditional introductory laboratory courses with research-based experiences that would inspire freshman students and promote STEM retention.
evidence: This references recommendations from the PCAST report.

claim: More than 5000 students—primarily freshmen—at 74 institutions have been involved since inception of the SEA-PHAGES program in 2008.
source: More than 5000 students—primarily freshmen—at 74 institutions have been involved since inception of the SEA-PHAGES program in 2008, and the phages isolated represent a broad geographical distribution (Figure 1) and a variety of viral morphotypes (http://phagesdb.org).
evidence: This is a factual statement about program participation.

claim: The phages isolated in the SEA-PHAGES program represent a broad geographical distribution.
source: More than 5000 students—primarily freshmen—at 74 institutions have been involved since inception of the SEA-PHAGES program in 2008, and the phages isolated represent a broad geographical distribution (Figure 1) and a variety of viral morphotypes (http://phagesdb.org).
evidence: This is supported by data and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The phages isolated in the SEA-PHAGES program represent a variety of viral morphotypes.
source: More than 5000 students—primarily freshmen—at 74 institutions have been involved since inception of the SEA-PHAGES program in 2008, and the phages isolated represent a broad geographical distribution (Figure 1) and a variety of viral morphotypes (http://phagesdb.org).
evidence: This is supported by data available at phagesdb.org.

claim: Using previously reported parameters based primarily on nucleotide sequence similarity spanning >50% genome length, the 627 genomes were assembled into 20 clusters (A–T) and eight singletons.
source: Using previously reported parameters based primarily on nucleotide sequence similarity spanning >50% genome length (Hatfull et al., 2006), the 627 genomes were assembled into 20 clusters (A–T) and eight singletons (with no close relatives) (Figure 2, Supplementary file 1); 11 clusters were subdivided into 2 to 11 subclusters (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis using established parameters, with results shown in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: 11 mycobacteriophage clusters were subdivided into 2 to 11 subclusters.
source: Using previously reported parameters based primarily on nucleotide sequence similarity spanning >50% genome length (Hatfull et al., 2006), the 627 genomes were assembled into 20 clusters (A–T) and eight singletons (with no close relatives) (Figure 2, Supplementary file 1); 11 clusters were subdivided into 2 to 11 subclusters (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis results shown in Table 1.

claim: There is considerable variation in cluster size with substantial differences in the numbers of genomes in each cluster (2–232).
source: There is considerable variation in cluster size with substantial differences in the numbers of genomes in each cluster (2–232), but there is relatively little variation in either genome length or the numbers of genes per genome in any given cluster (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on data shown in Table 1.

claim: There is relatively little variation in either genome length or the numbers of genes per genome in any given mycobacteriophage cluster.
source: There is considerable variation in cluster size with substantial differences in the numbers of genomes in each cluster (2–232), but there is relatively little variation in either genome length or the numbers of genes per genome in any given cluster (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on data shown in Table 1.

claim: Cluster A phages are similar in size and transcriptional organization, and share an unusual immunity system.
source: For example, Cluster A phages are similar in size and transcriptional organization, and share an unusual immunity system (Brown et al., 1997; Pope et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brown et al., 1997; Pope et al., 2011b.

claim: Cluster M phages all contain large numbers of tRNA genes.
source: Cluster M phages all contain large numbers of tRNA genes (Pope et al., 2014a), Cluster K (Pope et al., 2011a) and Cluster O (Cresawn et al., 2015) phages have different but characteristic repeated sequences, and Cluster J phages have an unusual capsid with a triangulation (T) number of 13 (Pope et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pope et al., 2014a.

claim: Cluster K and Cluster O phages have different but characteristic repeated sequences.
source: Cluster M phages all contain large numbers of tRNA genes (Pope et al., 2014a), Cluster K (Pope et al., 2011a) and Cluster O (Cresawn et al., 2015) phages have different but characteristic repeated sequences, and Cluster J phages have an unusual capsid with a triangulation (T) number of 13 (Pope et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pope et al., 2011a and Cresawn et al., 2015.

claim: Cluster J phages have an unusual capsid with a triangulation (T) number of 13.
source: Cluster M phages all contain large numbers of tRNA genes (Pope et al., 2014a), Cluster K (Pope et al., 2011a) and Cluster O (Cresawn et al., 2015) phages have different but characteristic repeated sequences, and Cluster J phages have an unusual capsid with a triangulation (T) number of 13 (Pope et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pope et al., 2013.

claim: The 69,633 genes from 627 mycobacteriophages assembled into 5205 phams.
source: The 69,633 genes assembled into 5205 phams of which 1613 (31%) are orphams (single-gene phamilies [Hatfull et al., 2010]).
evidence: This is a direct result from the pham assembly analysis.

claim: 1613 (31%) of the mycobacteriophage phams are orphams (single-gene phamilies).
source: The 69,633 genes assembled into 5205 phams of which 1613 (31%) are orphams (single-gene phamilies [Hatfull et al., 2010]).
evidence: This is a direct result from the pham assembly analysis.

claim: Approximately 25% of mycobacteriophage phams can be assigned functions in viral structure and assembly, DNA metabolism, integration, lysis, and regulation.
source: Approximately 25% of phams can be assigned functions in viral structure and assembly, DNA metabolism, integration, lysis, and regulation, but the vast majority are of unknown function.
evidence: This is based on functional annotation of the phams.

claim: The vast majority of mycobacteriophage phams are of unknown function.
source: Approximately 25% of phams can be assigned functions in viral structure and assembly, DNA metabolism, integration, lysis, and regulation, but the vast majority are of unknown function.
evidence: This is based on functional annotation of the phams.

claim: Representation of gene content relationships among all 627 phages as a network phylogeny reveals relationships that are in accord with the cluster and subcluster designations derived from nucleotide sequence comparisons.
source: Representation of gene content relationships among all 627 phages as a network phylogeny reveals relationships that are in accord with the cluster and subcluster designations derived from nucleotide sequence comparisons (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on network phylogeny analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The heat map strikingly illustrates that diversity is non-uniform, with genomes in some clusters being very closely related, whereas in others they display substantial differences.
source: The heat map strikingly illustrates that diversity is non-uniform, with genomes in some clusters (e.g., Subclusters B1, C1) being very closely related, whereas in others they display substantial differences (e.g., Subclusters A1, F1).
evidence: This is based on the heat map analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: 84.6% of Cluster C gene phamilies are found only in Cluster C and not elsewhere.
source: For example, at one extreme, 84.6% of Cluster C gene phamilies are found only in Cluster C and not elsewhere.
evidence: This is based on the Cluster Isolation Index (CII) calculation.

claim: Only 23.8% of Cluster I gene phamilies are constrained to that cluster, with the remainder having relatives present in genomes in other clusters.
source: At the other extreme, only 23.8% of Cluster I gene phamilies are constrained to that cluster, with the remainder having relatives present in genomes in other clusters.
evidence: This is based on the Cluster Isolation Index (CII) calculation.

claim: The singleton Dori shares 20–26% of its genes with Cluster B phages.
source: For example, the singleton Dori is clearly related to Cluster B phages (Figure 3) with which it shares limited DNA similarity (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) with 20–26% of its genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), but also has nucleotide similarity and shares genes with Cluster N and I2 phages, among others (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), as reflected in its low CII (Table 1, Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on gene content comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The singleton MooMoo shares approximately 20% of its gene content with Cluster F phages.
source: Likewise, the singleton MooMoo has segments of DNA similarity and shares ∼20% of its gene content (as determined by shared phams) with Cluster F phages (Figure 3, Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), but also has similarity to Clusters N and I, as well as a low CII (Table 1, Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on gene content comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: MooMoo has the same unusual prolate morphology as Cluster O phages.
source: It has low DNA similarity to Cluster O (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), but has several phams in common with the Cluster O phages, and has the same unusual prolate morphology (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on morphological observation shown in Figure 3.

claim: Mycobacteriophage Patience has a substantially lower GC% than its host (50.3% vs 67.4%).
source: We recently reported genomic analysis of the singleton mycobacteriophage Patience, which has a substantially lower GC% than its host (50.3% vs 67.4%), has a different codon usage profile, but is undergoing codon selection for growth in a high GC% environment (Pope et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pope et al., 2014b.

claim: Mycobacteriophage Patience has a different codon usage profile than its host but is undergoing codon selection for growth in a high GC% environment.
source: We recently reported genomic analysis of the singleton mycobacteriophage Patience, which has a substantially lower GC% than its host (50.3% vs 67.4%), has a different codon usage profile, but is undergoing codon selection for growth in a high GC% environment (Pope et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pope et al., 2014b.

claim: If there is a flux of phage genomes and genes entering the mycobacterial neighborhood, then the phages of a single host do not reflect a closed system with discrete populations, but one that is open with ever-expanding diversity.
source: If there is a flux of phage genomes and genes entering the mycobacterial neighborhood, then we predict that the phages of a single host do not reflect a closed system with discrete populations, but one that is open with ever-expanding diversity.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the observed gene flux.

claim: The rarefaction curves of the entire mycobacteriophage collection do not fit a hyperbola as would be expected if the mycobacteriophages were limited to an isolated set of genes.
source: Remarkably, the rarefaction curves of the entire collection—including the 95% confidence limits—do not fit a hyperbola as would be expected if the mycobacteriophages were limited to an isolated set of genes, and about 2.5 new gene phamilies are predicted to be identified with each newly isolated phage (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is based on rarefaction analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: About 2.5 new gene phamilies are predicted to be identified with each newly isolated mycobacteriophage.
source: Remarkably, the rarefaction curves of the entire collection—including the 95% confidence limits—do not fit a hyperbola as would be expected if the mycobacteriophages were limited to an isolated set of genes, and about 2.5 new gene phamilies are predicted to be identified with each newly isolated phage (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is based on rarefaction analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Similar independent analyses on the phages of Cluster A or the phages of Cluster B show that the lack of hyperbolic fit is also observed within these clusters.
source: Similar independent analyses on the phages of Cluster A or the phages of Cluster B show that this is also observed within these clusters (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: This is based on rarefaction analysis shown in Figure 7B,C.

claim: Both individual mycobacteriophage clusters and the collection as a whole are not genetically fixed, but are in constant flux.
source: Thus both individual clusters and the collection as a whole are not genetically fixed, but are in constant flux.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the rarefaction analysis results.

claim: The addition of a linear term representing the introduction of new phamilies from outside sources results in a non-asymptotic curve which predicts the continual identification of new phams even after large numbers of genomes have been sampled.
source: The addition of a linear term (see 'Materials and methods'), representing the introduction of new phamilies from outside sources, results in a non-asymptotic curve which predicts the continual identification of new phams even after large numbers of genomes have been sampled (R > 0.999; Figure 7D).
evidence: This is based on mathematical modeling shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The current dataset remains insufficient to confidently extrapolate to give an estimate of the total number of viral protein families in the biosphere.
source: Unfortunately, the current dataset remains insufficient to confidently extrapolate to give an estimate of the total number of viral protein families in the biosphere, which has been previously estimated to be anywhere between a half a million and 2 billion (Rohwer, 2003; Ignacio-Espinoza et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current analysis.

claim: The total number of viral protein families in the biosphere has been previously estimated to be anywhere between a half a million and 2 billion.
source: Unfortunately, the current dataset remains insufficient to confidently extrapolate to give an estimate of the total number of viral protein families in the biosphere, which has been previously estimated to be anywhere between a half a million and 2 billion (Rohwer, 2003; Ignacio-Espinoza et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rohwer, 2003; Ignacio-Espinoza et al., 2013.

claim: All double-stranded DNA tailed phage genomes in GenBank total 1781, corresponding to about 120 host bacterial genera, with a median number of phages per host genus of two.
source: We retrieved all double-stranded DNA tailed phage genomes in GenBank that we could identify (a total of 1781), corresponding to about 120 host bacterial genera, with a median number of phages per host genus of two.
evidence: This is based on data retrieval from GenBank.

claim: The 181,717 predicted genes from all double-stranded DNA tailed phages in GenBank assemble into 47,479 phamilies.
source: Using similar parameters for pham building as described above, the 181,717 predicted genes assemble into 47,479 phamilies.
evidence: This is based on pham assembly analysis of GenBank phage genomes.

claim: The relatively low representation of each phamily (3.8 genes/phamily) compared to the mycobacteriophages (13.4 genes/phamily) is a further reflection of the gross under-sampling of the phage population as a whole.
source: The relatively low representation of each phamily (3.8 genes/phamily) compared to the mycobacteriophages (13.4 genes/phamily) is a further reflection of the gross under-sampling of the phage population as a whole.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of pham representation.

claim: The mycobacteriophage myoviruses have a high CII and form a discrete group.
source: We also note that the mycobacteriophage myoviruses have a high CII and form a discrete group (Table 1) as do the Synechococcus myophages (Deng et al., 2014), perhaps reflecting a virulent lifestyle that constrains productive gene exchange; T4-related phages from diverse hosts share a core set of 15–20% of their genes, and whole genome comparisons reveal extensive mosaicism (Petrov et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on CII analysis shown in Table 1 and comparison with cited literature.

claim: The Synechococcus myophages form a discrete group.
source: We also note that the mycobacteriophage myoviruses have a high CII and form a discrete group (Table 1) as do the Synechococcus myophages (Deng et al., 2014), perhaps reflecting a virulent lifestyle that constrains productive gene exchange; T4-related phages from diverse hosts share a core set of 15–20% of their genes, and whole genome comparisons reveal extensive mosaicism (Petrov et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Deng et al., 2014.

claim: T4-related phages from diverse hosts share a core set of 15–20% of their genes.
source: We also note that the mycobacteriophage myoviruses have a high CII and form a discrete group (Table 1) as do the Synechococcus myophages (Deng et al., 2014), perhaps reflecting a virulent lifestyle that constrains productive gene exchange; T4-related phages from diverse hosts share a core set of 15–20% of their genes, and whole genome comparisons reveal extensive mosaicism (Petrov et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Petrov et al., 2010.

claim: Whole genome comparisons of T4-related phages reveal extensive mosaicism.
source: We also note that the mycobacteriophage myoviruses have a high CII and form a discrete group (Table 1) as do the Synechococcus myophages (Deng et al., 2014), perhaps reflecting a virulent lifestyle that constrains productive gene exchange; T4-related phages from diverse hosts share a core set of 15–20% of their genes, and whole genome comparisons reveal extensive mosaicism (Petrov et al., 2010).
